item.title: Measuring Colombia's Informal Output: Relative Earnings and Identification in a Bayesian Two-Sector Model, 1993-2026
item.description: arXiv:2611.28297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much of Colombia's measured output is produced by informal work? The answer cannot be read from the labor-informality rate: Colombia combines an informality rate above 50% with a much smaller informal share of output, because informal work is less productive. We estimate a Bayesian two-sector business-cycle model on quarterly national accounts and on reconstructed employment and informality series for 1993-2026. Identification comes from a new quarterly series of informal-to-formal labor earnings built from household-survey microdata for 2007-2026. Formal production uses capital and labor, informal production is labor based, and an accounting relationship maps relative earnings, the informality rate and the formal capital share into the informal output share. We show that aggregate data alone cannot pin down the size of the informal sector, and that relative earnings identify its quarterly path: from 2007 the path is invariant, within 0.3 percentage points, to the model's steady state. The informal share declines from about 30% of GDP in 1993 to 20% in 2026Q2, while labor informality falls from about 69% to 54%. The estimates lie within the range of published shadow-economy series for Colombia, close to the enhanced MIMIC estimates of Asllani, Dell'Anno and Schneider for 2009-2020. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the role of the capital share and of non-wage labor costs.
item.dc:creator: Jaime Vera-Jaramillo

item.title: Decision Theory with Degree of Membership in the State Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.28457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical decision theory considers a decision maker (DM) who faces a choice set C and believes that the true state of nature s* lies in a state space S. An objective function w(., .): C x S -> R1 maps actions and states into welfare. The DM wants to maximize w(., s*) but does not know s*. The state space specifies a labeled set of possible states. Possibility is binary: every state in S is possible and no state outside of S is possible. Thinking that this binary perspective on possibility is too rigid, we generalize the classical theory. We begin with a universe of labeled states U and a residual unlabeled state r. Classical theory associates a binary possibility indicator mu(s) with each s in (U, r). The residual state r is not possible, so mu(r) = 0. The state space is S = [s in U: mu(s) = 1]. We expand the range of mu to be the interval [0, 1]. Thus, mu is now a real number measuring degree of membership, a term we adopt from fuzzy set theory. The membership function mu(.): (U, r) -> [0, 1] differs substantively from but is consistent with the subjective probability distributions of Bayesian decision theory. Bayesian theory places a subjective distribution on the elements of a classical state space, each of whose members has degree of membership one. Degree of membership expresses the distinct idea that a DM may want to quantitatively express uncertainty regarding the composition of the state space. A mathematical distinction between subjective probabilities and degrees of membership is that the former must sum to one, but the latter need not. After formalizing basic ideas, we extend three prominent classical decision criteria--maximization of subjective expected welfare, minimax regret, and maximin--to our generalization of classical decision theory.
item.dc:creator: Jeff Dominitz, Charles F. Manski

item.title: Quadratic Forms of Multivariate $t$-Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.29074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper concerns quadratic forms of multivariate $t$-distributions. This paper derives the joint distribution and density of multiple quadratic forms, and establishes the possibility of a finite series approximation to the CDF. The paper also provides closed-form expressions for all the mixed moments that exist. Inverses of quadratic forms and ratios of quadratic forms are also considered.
item.dc:creator: Brendan Kline

item.title: Probability-Feasible Historical Transport: Sharp Bounds and Falsification Tests for Distributional Pre-Trend Designs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributional difference-in-differences studies often assume that the post-policy gap between treated and comparison groups is a mixture of pre-policy gaps. This historical-transport assumption can fail in ways that one-statistic checks miss. When policy events are pooled, the average counterfactual can be a valid distribution although no event's counterfactual is, and pooled bounds can exclude the true average effect. Mixtures of past gaps can assign negative probability to outcomes, and cutoff-by-cutoff bounds can be incompatible. We characterize sharp bounds and give breakdown radii, a grid-free confidence region, and tests with and without an experiment. The tests reject transport in the National Supported Work data and expose impossible state counterfactuals behind a pooled minimum-wage bound. For the 1993 Earned Income Tax Credit expansion they pass through 1995, when bounds put single mothers' employment gain relative to childless women at 5 to 7 points; the gain stays positive after dropping early welfare-waiver states.
item.dc:creator: Ulrich Hounyo

item.title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.29747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.
item.dc:creator: Sander Barendse, Ming Cheng

item.title: Shadow economy as a null set. Measure-theoretic approach to shadow economy
item.description: arXiv:2611.29797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we asked if the shadow economy can be defined as a system of null sets for institutional measures or sensors that measure economic transactions. As an answer a measure-theoretic testable framework to redefine and quantify the shadow economy was designed. Traditional economic definitions frequently conflate the actual shadow economy with the observational limitations of state institutions. To resolve this, we model the shadow economy as a null set relative to institutional measures and analyze three complementary economic regimes. We explore in this context how standard mathematical tools can be given economic meaning. First, in the low-resolution regime, we apply Banach Lattices and Lebesgue decomposition of a measure to address transaction underreporting by aggregating incomplete institutional registries using a supremum fusion operator. Second, for hidden economic dimensions, we utilize Copula theory and Kullback-Leibler divergence optimization to reconstruct unobserved financial flows from technological and physical indicators. Third, we address audit scalability by modeling the shadow economy as a sparse vector, applying Compressed Sensing to detect high-volume sparse evasion networks through random, incoherent, and privacy-preserving sampling.
item.dc:creator: Rados\l{}aw A. Kycia, Andrzej Buszko

item.title: The Entangled Veil: Why Redistribution Requires a New Language
item.description: arXiv:2611.30045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Rawlsian veil of ignorance requires choosing principles of justice without knowing which position-temporal, spatial, social, or personal one will occupy. We argue that this object cannot be represented faithfully within standard economic models. A faithful representation must satisfy three requirements: it must treat all generations symmetrically, capture non-separable correlations among positions, and allow mobility costs to vary across locations and occupations. We show that standard optimal-tax models violate at least one requirement, and that the minimal framework satisfying all three is a geometric framework adapted from string theory, in which the veil is an entangled state over a space of possible life situations. We derive full equalization as a first-best benchmark, the emergence of separated clusters when correlations reward distinction, a symmetry between intraand inter-generational equity, and a tunneling mechanism by which correlations reduce institutional barriers. The model generates four inequality profiles and four inequality types. The estimates are quantitatively important: the framework changes the ranking of redistributive policies, and ignoring the margins it identifies leads to systematically biased policy evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Nazaria Solferino, Viviana Solferino

item.title: Adaptive experiments with observational data: Efficient experimental design and asymptotic time-uniform inference for long-term treatment effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.30595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects in experiments requires waiting for outcomes to become observable, which can delay both the evaluation of an intervention and subsequent decisions. Recent econometric work has developed identification methods that combine experimental data with observational data containing long-term outcomes. This paper proposes using observational data available before the experiment begins not only for identification but also for designing adaptive experiments, in which experimental data are collected sequentially. To estimate the long-term average treatment effect as precisely as possible, we express its semiparametric efficiency bound as a function of the covariate sampling and treatment assignment rules and minimize the bound over these rules to characterize an optimal fixed experimental design. This experimental design depends on the treatment-specific conditional variances of the observational prediction of the long-term outcome, which can be learned only from experimental participants. We therefore construct a sequential procedure that learns the experimental design as experimental data accumulate and show that its estimator attains the same limiting variance as an oracle estimator implemented under the optimal fixed experimental design. We further construct an asymptotic confidence sequence whose coverage holds simultaneously over all rounds after a prespecified start, so that the experimenter can inspect the interval after each participant and stop once it excludes zero. Monte Carlo simulations show that the learned experimental design can improve precision and shorten the time to detection relative to baseline sampling and equal-probability assignment. An illustration using the Pakistan Graduation experiment shows how estimated conditional variance heterogeneity informs sampling and treatment assignment.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Kawato

item.title: What Should an Experiment Measure? Combining a Short-Term Experiment with Confounded Observational Data to Identify Long-Term Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.30599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observational data often record long-term outcomes but do not identify long-term treatment effects when selection depends on unrecorded characteristics, while randomized experiments remove this selection but require years of follow-up. We ask what a short-term experiment should measure so that, combined with observational data, it identifies the average long-term treatment effect in the observational population. In our main setting, the observational data record a coarse post-treatment measurement of the unrecorded characteristics but not a detailed measurement that would remove confounding. In this setting, we derive three implications for what the experiment should measure. It should (1) collect the same coarse measurement, (2) measure the characteristics in enough detail that conditioning on this detailed measurement and recorded covariates removes confounding and leaves the coarse measurement uninformative about selection and the treatment-specific long-term outcome mean, and (3) distinguish no more levels of the characteristics than the coarse measurement can separate. We characterize the treatment effect through linear inverse problems based on exclusion restrictions and completeness, and thereby show that combining such an experiment with the observational data identifies the effect. We propose an estimator that is based on the efficient influence function and removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation errors. We give conditions under which this estimator is asymptotically normal and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Cross-fitting relaxes the conditions on nuisance estimation. In simulations and a Job Corps illustration, the proposed Tikhonov-penalized series estimator has smaller absolute bias and coverage closer to the nominal level than competing estimators.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Kawato

item.title: Spurious Information in Large Markets: Random Matrix Laws for Entropy, Mutual Information and the Value of Information
item.description: arXiv:2611.30998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence and mutual information have become standard currencies for measuring how much one set of financial variables reveals about another. In large cross-sections they are almost always computed from sample covariance matrices, and the noise in those matrices is the object of random matrix theory. This paper develops the random matrix theory of Gaussian information functionals and applies it to markets. I show that the plug-in mutual information between two blocks of p and r variables estimated from $n$ observations has an exact expected excess, the spurious information, that is a digamma telescope independent of the true dependence. Under independence its law is that of a product of Beta variables. In the proportional regime it grows linearly with an order-one variance. The same quantity is a linear spectral statistic of the Jacobi ensemble, which yields a closed form for the logarithmic moment of Wachter's law. Spurious information increases strictly whenever uninformative coordinates are added. In a CARA-Gaussian economy the certainty-equivalent value of a signal equals mutual information divided by risk aversion, so these results translate one for one into a spurious value of information. The canonical-correlation phase transition then defines a frontier of minimum detectable information. On daily returns of 49 US industry portfolios from 1990 to 2026, I document the market mode, the reliability of sector eigenvectors implied by the BBP transition, the out-of-sample cost of noise dressing, and an information linkage between carbon-intensive and financial industries that survives exact bias correction and conditioning on the market.
item.dc:creator: James Rice

item.title: Skew-Symmetric Factor Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The paper introduces and analyzes a factor model for (real) skew-symmetric data, which arise naturally in directed flows and in pairwise comparisons used for rankings. Working within a signal-plus-noise framework, we analyze spectral inference and establish a BBP-type phase transition in signal strength. Under Gaussian noise, we derive joint eigenvalue fluctuation limits. Above the separation threshold, the estimated signal strength is asymptotically normal whenever the population strength has multiplicity one. For a general multiplicity $k$, the joint limiting fluctuations of the corresponding sample eigenvalues above the threshold are given by the eigenvalues of a scaled $k\times k$ Gaussian unitary ensemble matrix. The skew-symmetric structure induces paired eigenspaces, and we characterize the canonical angles between the population and sample eigenspaces. Below the threshold, the corresponding largest sample eigenvalue converges to the edge of the semicircle law, with fluctuations governed by the Tracy--Widom $F_2$ distribution, in contrast to the $F_1$ law familiar from real symmetric models. The approach is illustrated through financial and demographic applications.
item.dc:creator: Anna Bykhovskaya, Tomas Espana, Jianqing Fan

item.title: Computational Strategies for Mixed Logit Estimation Automatic Differentiation, GPU Computing, and Floating-Point Precision
item.description: arXiv:2611.29833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mixed logit estimation can become computationally demanding as sample size and the dimension of preference heterogeneity increase. This study examines how derivative computation, processor choice and floating-point precision affect estimation time and parameter recovery across problem sizes. This paper provides a controlled benchmark, comparing finite differences (FD) with automatic differentiation (AD), central processing unit (CPU) execution with graphics processing unit (GPU) execution, and double-precision (FP64) with single-precision (FP32) arithmetic using Monte Carlo experiments that hold the data-generating process, simulation draws, optimiser, starting values, and objective function fixed across strategies. The results show that AD is the dominant source of acceleration. Combining AD with FP32 arithmetic provides further gains, while combining AD, GPU execution, and FP32 arithmetic delivers the largest speed improvements, particularly as sample size and model complexity increase. Our findings indicate substantial computational gains with broadly comparable parameter-recovery performance in the simulated settings considered.An empirical application in health preferences illustrates what extra empirical evidence and statistical benefit on model fit could be achieved, when researchers are made possible to estimate a richer, correlated preference specification. We provide an open sourced prototype to for model estimation with AD-FP32 strategy workflow that automatically detect hardware and provide the fastest estimation. Faster estimation can make richer random-coefficient specifications, larger simulation draw counts, bootstrap inference, multi-start optimisation, and robustness checks more feasible in applied choice modelling research.
item.dc:creator: Hengzhe Zhao Jinhui Zhang Yuanyuan Gu

item.title: Sensitivity Analysis in Unconditional Quantile Effects
item.description: arXiv:2303.14298v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes a framework to analyze the effects of counterfactual policies on the unconditional quantiles of an outcome variable. For a given counterfactual policy, we obtain identified sets for the effect of both marginal and global changes in the proportion of treated individuals. To conduct a sensitivity analysis, we introduce the quantile breakdown frontier, a curve that $(i)$ indicates whether a sensitivity analysis is possible or not, and $(ii)$ when a sensitivity analysis is possible, quantifies the amount of selection bias consistent with a given conclusion of interest across different quantiles. To illustrate our method, we perform a sensitivity analysis on the effect of unionizing low income workers on the quantiles of the distribution of (log) wages.
item.dc:creator: Julian Martinez-Iriarte

item.title: Inference in clustered IV models with many and weak instruments
item.description: arXiv:2306.08559v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies inference in instrumental variable models with many, weak instruments and clustered data. It first examines how clustering affects identification strength, showing how to adapt the concentration parameter to account for within-cluster dependence. The adapted concentration parameter may be smaller and may grow more slowly asymptotically than the concentration parameter that ignores the dependence, thereby weakening identification. Next, the paper extends the identification-robust jackknife Anderson--Rubin and jackknife score statistics for independent data to clustered data by removing clusters rather than individual observations from the statistics. These statistics converge jointly to a normal distribution under many-instrument asymptotics, such that scaling with cluster cross-fit variance estimators yields identification-robust tests. Simulations show that the cluster jackknife tests achieve close to nominal size and have good power. A reanalysis of a study on the effect of queenly reign on war shows the empirical relevance of the new tests.
item.dc:creator: Johannes W. Ligtenberg

item.title: Identification of Heterogeneous Peer Effects
item.description: arXiv:2410.14317v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a peer effects model in which each peer's influence depends on their outcome rank within the peer group. Unlike existing models, it allows non-monotonic effects across ranks. The model admits a unique equilibrium, and its parameters can be identified using peers' exogenous characteristics. We introduce a parsimonious quantile-dependent specification and develop a specification test to guide model selection. Applying the model to student outcomes in Add Health reveals heterogeneous, often non-monotonic spillovers. Counterfactual analysis shows that allowing for non-monotonic peer effects changes the rankings of influential students relative to existing models. Our R package, QuantilePeer, implements these methods.
item.dc:creator: Eyo I. Herstad, Aristide Houndetoungan, Myungkou Shin

item.title: Estimation and Inference for the $\tau$-Quantile of Heterogeneous Individual-Specific Coefficient
item.description: arXiv:2605.01923v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study quantiles of heterogeneous coefficients across the $n$ observed units of a panel. Treating the coefficients as deterministic, we estimate each from $T$ observations, then use the estimates and their standard errors to construct a smoothed quantile estimator and estimate its variance. When $T^{1/2}\ll n\ll T^{3/2}$, the estimator is asymptotically normal around a deterministic center. A feasible bias correction relaxes the sample growth restriction to $n/T^{3/2}\to c\in[0,\infty)$, accommodating panels with large $n$. Normal inference extends to the target quantile when the difference between the deterministic center and the target is negligible relative to the standard error. Without this restriction, we establish an impossibility result that the distribution of the studentized error relative to the target cannot be estimated uniformly consistently. For practical inference in this case, we construct a conservative interval whose coverage tends uniformly to one and whose length attains the optimal worst-case rate in probability. We give primitive conditions for smooth GMM. Mortgage data show widespread but uneven declines in delinquency across credit scores.
item.dc:creator: Antonio F. Galvao, Ulrich Hounyo, Jiahao Lin

item.title: When the Scaffold Stays On: AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation
item.description: arXiv:2606.06253v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative AI can perform many of the tasks through which programmers build skill. When it substitutes for practice, skill development suffers; when it complements practice, learning may accelerate. Therefore, one programmer in the substitute mode and another in the complement mode can produce the same AI-assisted output yet differ in the skill they have acquired. We ask what digital practice records reveal about skill formation and whether AI-prohibited evaluations help distinguish the two modes of AI use. We follow 10,419 users of Codeforces (CF), an open, unproctored programming practice and contest platform with no enforced restriction on AI assistance, from 2018 to 2025. We link them to the rosters of the International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI), which admit entrants through qualification rounds and prohibit AI under in-person proctoring. From CF practice telemetry, we construct an AI-prompt signature (higher first-attempt acceptance rates, fewer attempts per solved problem, and fewer rapid debugging retries), consistent with AI-assisted practice. Three patterns emerge. Practice shifted toward the signature across entry cohorts spanning the releases of GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT. On CF, a stronger signature is associated with slower skill growth among users not linked to ICPC or IOI rosters, but not among roster-linked users. Among AI-era entrants who reached ICPC, larger within-user shifts toward the signature are positively associated with non-AI performance. These patterns are consistent with qualification screening on acquired skill, which admits users who complement practice with AI and excludes those who substitute AI for practice.
item.dc:creator: Song Yao

item.title: Robust Signal Maximization in Spillover Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2607.18601v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the optimal design and analysis of experiments for estimating spillover effects. Assuming a known (e.g., linear) exposure mapping, we characterize the treatment-assignment distribution and regression-based estimator that minimize worst-case approximate variance against a broad class of distributions of unobservables. The design problem yields an intuitive solution in which the planner trades off spillover signal strength against dispersion of spillover variation. The analysis problem yields a simple recentered instrumental variable estimator to best leverage this variation. This framework produces natural solutions in several benchmark cases - such as clustered exposure - and suggests computationally tractable approximations for general networks, including bipartite settings. We illustrate these new tools in semi-synthetic experiments based on three applications from development economics. Our approach yields large standard error reductions in these experiments, increasing effective sample sizes by 44-266%.
item.dc:creator: Kirill Borusyak, Peter Hull, Evan Munro

item.title: Uniform Inference for Parameters Identified by Conditional Quantile Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2609.23303v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many structural and dynamic economic models imply that key parameters are identified by conditional quantile restrictions. Building on the exponential weighting approach of Bierens (1990) and the penalized maximum statistics of Chen et al. (2025), we develop a uniform inference method for such parameters. We construct an adaptive $\ell_1$-penalized statistic from a process indexed by quantiles and weighting directions. The statistic aggregates evidence across quantiles and regularizes maximization over directions. A shifted bootstrap is used to estimate local power for penalty selection. Under the stated conditions, adaptive selection asymptotically preserves or improves worst case local power relative to the unpenalized test over a prespecified set of alternatives. The improvement is strict when a positive candidate penalty raises the population level criterion above its value at zero. We also extend the process and bootstrap theory to the setting with pre-estimated nuisance parameters. We characterize their contribution to the limiting process, correct the variance estimator, and establish Gaussian multiplier bootstrap validity for null inference. Monte Carlo experiments favor the CvM-KS method for size control under pre-estimation and show that adaptive penalization can improve empirical power relative to the unpenalized test.
item.dc:creator: Xuqing Lin, Xiaojun Song

item.title: Bias Correction and Inference for Panel Quantile Regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.36443v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a large-$n$, large-$T$ theory for the unsmoothed fixed-effects quantile regression estimator that allows for serially correlated panel data. An exact rank-score identity for the profiled criterion, with a convexity argument, delivers the leading incidental parameter bias of the slope estimator, of order $T^{-1}$, in closed form, paralleling Hahn and Newey (2004) for smooth nonlinear panel models. When $n$ and $T$ grow at the same rate, the estimator is asymptotically normal but in general not centred, and conventional intervals are invalid. In stationary panels whose dependence decays geometrically or polynomially, with $n/T$ bounded, serial correlation changes the structure of this bias: the long-run variance of the quantile score enters it, and feedback from past errors to current regressors adds a term that can bias the estimator even at the median. A split-panel jackknife with contiguous half-panels removes the bias, whereas one with interleaved half-panels does not in general, and a cluster-robust variance estimator, clustered by individual, yields valid inference. Under independence over time, the admissible growth of $n$ relative to $T$, up to $n=o(T^3)$, depends on the regularity of the conditional error densities, and the jackknife is valid throughout this range.
item.dc:creator: Harold D Chiang, Wei Biao Wu

item.title: Time-Varying Quantile VAR Models: Estimation and Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.36634v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop an econometric framework for impulse response analysis in time-varying quantile vector autoregressive (TV-QVAR) models. Unlike standard conditional-mean setting, TV-QVAR systems face a fundamental analytical challenge: neither time-varying parameters nor conditional quantiles propagate linearly through dynamic recursions. To overcome this, we establish a uniform Bahadur representation for local quantile VAR estimation, propose a smoothed check-function approach for tractable parameter inference, and introduce the best linear projection of the time-varying quantile impulse response (TV-QIR) function to recover well-defined dynamic causal effects. Applying our methodology to U.S. industrial production growth and credit spreads from 1919 to 2025 uncovers pronounced structural shifts in tail interdependence, showing that downside asymmetry is concentrated at short horizons and diminishes as the forecast horizon lengthens.
item.dc:creator: Jiti Gao, Fei Liu, Bin Peng

item.title: Doubly robust estimation of direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
item.description: arXiv:2610.37049v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.
item.dc:creator: Martin Huber

item.title: Financial Volatility and Risk Forecasting Incorporating a Larger Number of Realized Measures
item.description: arXiv:2411.17136v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-frequency data have led to the development of numerous realized volatility measures, while standard Realized GARCH models typically rely on a single measure. This paper proposes three approaches to incorporate information from multiple realized measures within the Realized GARCH framework. First, we develop an autoencoder-enhanced Realized GARCH model that constructs a synthetic realized measure through nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Second, we propose a linear weighted Realized GARCH model that jointly estimates convex aggregation weights and model parameters. Third, we introduce a functional weighted Realized GARCH model based on parsimonious Beta weighting functions. Using approximately 22 years of data for 29 international equity indices, we evaluate the proposed methods in volatility, Value-at-Risk, and Expected Shortfall forecasting. Compared with benchmark models based on single realized measures, equal weighting, and linear dimension reduction, the proposed methods consistently deliver more accurate volatility and risk forecasts.
item.dc:creator: Qianli Zhao, Chao Wang, Richard Gerlach, Giuseppe Storti, Lingxiang Zhang

item.title: Multilevel non-linear interrupted time series analysis
item.description: arXiv:2511.05725v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in interrupted time series analysis permit characterization of a typical non-linear interruption effect through use of generalized additive models. Concurrently, advances in latent time series modeling allow efficient Bayesian multilevel time series models. We propose to combine these concepts with a hierarchical model selection prior to characterize interruption effects with a multilevel structure, encouraging parsimony and partial pooling while incorporating meaningful variability in causal effects across subpopulations of interest, while allowing poststratification. These models are demonstrated with three applications: 1) the effect of the introduction of the prostate specific antigen test on prostate cancer diagnosis rates by race and age group, 2) the change in stroke or trans-ischemic attack hospitalization rates across Medicare beneficiaries by rurality in the months after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and 3) the effect of Medicaid expansion in Missouri on the proportion of inpatient hospitalizations discharged with Medicaid as a primary payer by key age groupings and sex.
item.dc:creator: RJ Waken, Fengxian Wang, Sarah A. Eisenstein, Tim McBride, Kim Johnson, Karen Joynt-Maddox

item.title: Stochastic Deep Learning: A Probabilistic Framework for Modeling Uncertainty in Structured Temporal Data
item.description: arXiv:2601.05227v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: I propose a novel framework that integrates stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with deep generative models to improve uncertainty quantification in machine learning applications involving structured and temporal data. This approach, termed Stochastic Latent Differential Inference (SLDI), embeds an It\^o SDE in the latent space of a variational autoencoder, allowing for flexible, continuous-time modeling of uncertainty while preserving a principled mathematical foundation. The drift and diffusion terms of the SDE are parameterized by neural networks, enabling data-driven inference and generalizing classical time series models to handle irregular sampling and complex dynamic structure. A central theoretical contribution is the co-parameterization of the adjoint state with a dedicated neural network, forming a coupled forward-backward system that captures not only latent evolution but also gradient dynamics. I introduce a pathwise-regularized adjoint loss and analyze variance-reduced gradient flows through the lens of stochastic calculus, offering new tools for improving training stability in deep latent SDEs. My paper unifies and extends variational inference, continuous-time generative modeling, and control-theoretic optimization, providing a rigorous foundation for future developments in stochastic probabilistic machine learning.
item.dc:creator: James Rice

item.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
item.description: arXiv:2603.00041v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification. We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Petrungaro, Anthony C. Constantinou

item.title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2603.24705v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Discrete choice models are fundamental tools in management science, economics, and marketing. Logit models dominate applied work because they yield closed-form choice probabilities, but IID Gumbel errors impose restrictive substitution patterns. We propose an amortized inference approach based on a neural network emulator that approximates choice probabilities under general, potentially correlated, error distributions. We develop a specialized neural network architecture respecting the invariance properties of discrete choice models and provide group-theoretic foundations for universal approximation from a minimal set of invariant features. Using Sobolev training, the emulator learns choice probabilities and their derivatives, enabling rapid likelihood and gradient evaluation. We show that emulator-based maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal under mild approximation conditions. Simulations show substantial gains over the GHK simulator in accuracy and speed. Using NielsenIQ data on household laundry-detergent purchases, we estimate correlated-probit and correlated-Gumbel models with rich household-level random effects. The IID period-error restriction---and hence the conditional-IIA restriction underlying conventional mixed logit---is strongly rejected. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selects a correlated-Gumbel model with a three-factor period-error covariance structure. We find that allowing correlated period errors materially changes predicted product substitution patterns.
item.dc:creator: Easton Huch, Michael Keane

item.title: Coupling and Maximal Inequalities for Graph-Dependent Empirical Processes
item.description: arXiv:2606.31936v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop maximal inequalities for empirical processes indexed by graph-dependent observations. Our bounds separate the complexity of the indexing class from two features specific to graph dependence: the geometry of the underlying graph and the cost of coupling graph-separated blocks to independent copies. The coupling construction combines a novel graph-adapted dependence coefficient with a coloring of a block partition. As an application, we derive Glivenko--Cantelli results and characterize the associated effective sample size. A central implication is that graph-dependent empirical processes need not exhibit a generic root-$n$ rate: convergence is jointly determined by function-class complexity, graph geometry, and the decay of dependence with graph distance. We specialize the results to graphs with polynomial and exponential growth and to directed dyadic graphs. Finally, we apply the results to network autoregressive models, nonlinear local-propagation models, and treatment-interference settings.
item.dc:creator: Mengsi Gao, Demian Pouzo

item.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
item.description: arXiv:2611.26410v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $\beta$-H\"older source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Ballarin, Lukas Gonon, Lyudmila Grigoryeva
